transcript:
Header:
- Date: 2026-07-15
- Time: 15:00 - 16:05 UTC
- Duration: ~65 minutes
- Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (CTO, Cygnus), Arjun Patel (SRE), Sofia Ruiz (Head of ML), Tom Becker (Infra)

Auto-generated Summary:
- Goal: Understand p95/p99 tail latency issues and plan benchmarking to hit Cygnus SLA (~3s median, p99 < 5s)
- Immediate asks: traces, network diagram, benchmark scripts

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to do a deep dive on tail latency — p95 and p99 — and look at streaming versus non-streaming behaviors, plus kv cache, batching, quantization and any network hop effects you might be seeing.
[00:12] Maya Chen: Yeah thanks Lena, we, um, have been seeing fairly wide p99 spikes on our customer-facing QA endpoint. Median is fine but, like, p99 is all over the place.
[00:20] Diego Morales: Totally, and just to set expectations, we'll probably go through three layers: model/runtime characteristics, infra/network, and then configuration knobs (batching, cache, quant). We'll also propose a bench runbook.
[00:34] Arjun Patel: Quick context: our infra is in a VPC in GCP, fronted by a private ALB, and inference cluster is in a dedicated subnet; there are a couple of NAT hops for some telemetry to leave, but it's fairly closed. Typical RTTs between app tier and inference nodes are 8–12 ms.
[00:50] Priya Nair: Thanks Arjun. Two clarifications for the group: when you say p99 spikes, is that for streaming responses (chunked streaming) or non-streaming (single payload)?
[01:02] Sofia Ruiz: Mostly streaming; our chat UI renders as tokens arrive. But we've tried non-streaming mode for some heavy-batched jobs and saw different tail shapes.
[01:12] Diego Morales: Okay good, that's important. Streaming can mask downstream latency but also amplifies p99 in different ways — per-chunk commit points, client ACKs, and network backpressure.
[01:25] Tom Becker: We also noticed some correlation between long tail and cold cache behavior — first requests after autoscale or after evictions.
[01:33] Lena Park: Perfect. Let's jump into runtime. Diego, can you walk through KV cache and batching interactions?
[01:40] Diego Morales: Sure. Two main KV cache effects: prefix KV caching for repeated prompts and session KV for streaming continuations. If you have high reuse, kv hits drop decode time significantly. But miss patterns cause expensive recomputation for the full attention context and retrace through the model — that's where p95/p99 tails often come from.
[01:58] Diego Morales: Also, batching interacts: larger batches improve throughput but increase queuing latency for early-arriving requests — the classic tail-vs-median tradeoff. Redwood's runtime supports dynamic batching that tries to respect latency SLOs by adaptively closing micro-batches when a time threshold is hit, but that threshold tuning depends on your token length distribution.
[02:20] Maya Chen: Quick question: we have a bimodal token length distribution — most queries are 40–80 tokens but some go to 600 tokens. How should that shape batching settings?
[02:30] Priya Nair: Bimodal workloads are tricky. You can do size-based batch slicing: separate short from long requests into different queues or routes. Redwood supports routing policies to send long-context requests to dedicated pools or lower-priority queues to avoid tail amplification.
[02:43] Arjun Patel: In practice we've tried splitting on inferred length at edge, but it added complexity. Curious how much benefit we'd see versus complexity cost.
[02:52] Diego Morales: In our experience, separating long tails can reduce p99 noticeably without impacting median. For example, a 10–15% p99 reduction in similar workloads we've benchmarked. We'll provide an example config.
[03:05] Maya Chen: Okay. Next quantization: we've tested int8 on a stage model and saw slight quality degradation but big perf improvements. Any guidance on quant and tail behavior?
[03:16] Diego Morales: Quantization usually reduces per-token compute, which lowers median and tail compute times, but it can introduce variability due to different kernel paths and fallback code on some hardware — especially when using mixed precision and split kernels. For p99 it's important to benchmark with the exact quantization profile and library. Also watch for memory bandwidth stalls on some GPU types with int8.
[03:36] Priya Nair: Another note: certain 4-bit quantization modes can cause occasional longer tails if the runtime triggers a slow-path for rare op shapes. It's rare but observable.
[03:47] Tom Becker: Does Redwood's runtime emit a flag when slow-paths are taken?
[03:51] Diego Morales: Yes, at the moment we log kernel fallback events and expose them in tracing with tags like runtime.kernel_fallback=true, which you can collect in traces. We'll include those in the runbook.
[04:02] Lena Park: Let's talk streaming specifics — what are the common sources of p99 when streaming?
[04:06] Diego Morales: Streaming adds per-chunk overhead: chunk serialization, network flushes, and client ack waits. If your client reads slowly or there's backpressure, tokens can pile up in the server's send buffer causing head-of-line issues. Also, if the client maintains many concurrent streams, connection limits or HTTP/2 windowing can cause bursts.
[04:27] Sofia Ruiz: Our front-end does token-by-token rendering with short timeouts, but we do have spikes in concurrent sessions. Could that amplify tail?
[04:34] Priya Nair: Yes — concurrency multiplies effects. We usually recommend a hybrid: stream for low-latency UX, but fall back to short non-streamed chunks for high concurrency periods. 
[04:45] Diego Morales: Also, consider producing larger minimal chunks (e.g., 8–16 tokens) to reduce per-chunk overhead while keeping perceived latency low.
[04:53] Arjun Patel: About network hops: we measured 8–12 ms internal RTT, but some requests go through an internal NAT and telemetry path adding ~20–30 ms. Could that be the p99 culprit?
[05:05] Diego Morales: Definitely possible. Tail can be dominated by a small fraction of requests that traverse a slower network path or an overloaded NAT gateway. The classic pattern: 95% of requests take fast path, 5% take slow path — that becomes p99 if those slow ones are 10x slower.
[05:18] Lena Park: We should instrument per-hop timings and tag traces with route ids. Arjun, can you get us a topology and typical percentiles per hop?
[05:26] Arjun Patel: Yep, will add that to action items.
[05:29] Maya Chen: What about autoscaling and cold starts — we've seen spikes when new instances come up. How much of a factor is model load time?
[05:38] Diego Morales: Cold starts are huge if the model needs to be loaded from disk. Reducing cold start p99 can be done by pre-warming nodes, keeping an LRU of hot models in memory, or using fast-storage (NVMe). With dedicated pools you can configure minimum replica counts to reduce cold starts at cost of reserved capacity.
[05:55] Priya Nair: For Private deployments, consider pre-loading the model on a standby pool that receives warmup requests; Redwood Dedicated offers configurable min_replicas to balance cost and p99.
[06:06] Tom Becker: What about KV cache warmup? We saw the first 100 sessions are slow after a restart. Any best practices?
[06:13] Diego Morales: Warmup can be mitigated by synthetic pre-warm traffic using representative prefixes; also persistent KV stores or checkpointed KV caches across restarts help. The runtime supports rolling restarts to avoid full-cold windows.
[06:26] Maya Chen: Metrics — which ones should we monitor to really catch p99 causes?
[06:31] Diego Morales: Key metrics: per-request compute time, queue wait time, batch size, KV cache hit rate, kernel_fallback counts, GPU SM utilization, memory bandwidth saturation, per-hop network latency, and per-chunk send time for streaming. Also track distribution of token lengths and concurrency.
[06:48] Priya Nair: We also recommend histograms for batch wait times and per-stage latencies (ingest, queue, compute, encode, send).
[06:56] Arjun Patel: For benchmark methodology, what should we send you? We'll want to compare streaming vs non-streaming and quant profiles.
[07:03] Diego Morales: We'll provide a bench runbook that includes: synthetic runner that replays traces with original inter-arrival timings, separate runs for streaming chunk sizes (1, 8, 16 tokens) and non-streamed payloads, quantized vs FP16 runs, and both cold and warm cache scenarios. We'll include scripts to simulate client-side slow readers.
[07:22] Maya Chen: Great. Any quick wins we can apply right now?
[07:26] Lena Park: From what's been said: 1) increase min_replicas to reduce cold starts, 2) separate long-context requests into own pool, 3) bump chunk size for streaming to 8 tokens, 4) enable kernel fallback tracing, 5) gather traces and network topology.
[07:40] Sofia Ruiz: On quality, we need to keep an eye on quant-induced regressions. We'll only roll quant to production after evaluating eval sets.
[07:47] Diego Morales: Totally. We'll include evaluation hooks so you can compare generations across quant profiles and gating criteria.
[07:54] Tom Becker: One thing we saw: occasional GC pauses in the telemetry agent caused temporary stalls in the send pipeline. There's a small telemetry sidecar that flushes logs to an external endpoint — do you think that could block?
[08:06] Priya Nair: Sidecars can cause head-of-line blocking if they share the same CPU thread pool or network interface. Is the sidecar on the same pod?
[08:12] Tom Becker: Yes, same node sometimes.
[08:15] Diego Morales: If that's the case, isolate telemetry on a different NIC or use async buffered logging to avoid blocking the inference send path.
[08:24] Maya Chen: Any other observability suggestions?
[08:27] Diego Morales: Tag traces with model_version, quant_profile, batch_id, kv_hit boolean, and route_id. Then run flamegraphs for p99 to see whether compute or queue dominates.
[08:39] Priya Nair: We'll also recommend SLO-based alerting on the p99 of end-to-end latency, not just median.
[08:45] Lena Park: OK let's move to a few concrete configurations. Diego, can you walk through a recommended config for Cygnus' workload?
[08:52] Diego Morales: Sure. High-level: reserve a long-request pool with min_replicas=2, default pool min_replicas=4 to reduce cold starts during traffic spikes, dynamic batching with max_batch_time_ms=12 for default pool, and for long-pool use max_batch_time_ms=25 with batch slicing to limit token heterogeneity. For streaming, use chunk_size=8 tokens and enable buffered-async-send. For quant, test int8 with fallback to fp16 for critical ops and enable kernel_fallback_tracing.
[09:16] Arjun Patel: Those batching times — 12 ms seems aggressive; our current median is around 40 ms. Would that raise waste?
[09:23] Diego Morales: max_batch_time_ms should reflect your latency SLO and median. If median is 40 ms, you might choose a slightly higher threshold; it's a tuning knob. The point is to bound queueing latency so lots of requests don't wait indefinitely for batch fullness.
[09:35] Maya Chen: For private/on-prem installs, are there differences for network topology assumptions?
[09:40] Priya Nair: On-prem often has fewer network hops but potentially older NICs; tune NIC offloads and ensure RDMA or GPUDirect if available. Also consider colocating front-end and inference in the same rack to reduce hops.
[09:52] Sofia Ruiz: We might consider a private deployment for some regulated customers; any p99 tradeoffs there?
[09:58] Diego Morales: Private deployments can reduce unpredictable network hops (good for p99) but add operational burden. Using Redwood Private with the control plane managed and data plane in your VPC gives you the best of both in many cases.
[10:09] Maya Chen: Good to know. Let's capture the bench plan and responsibilities.
[10:14] Lena Park: Quick recap of next steps and owners — Diego will produce script and example configs; Maya and Arjun will share traces and topology; Lena will send security and deployment docs; we'll meet after initial bench results.
[10:25] Arjun Patel: Sounds good. Also, can Redwood share any historical p99 case studies?
[10:30] Diego Morales: Yes, we'll attach a couple of anonymized case studies showing config changes and p99 improvements.
[10:36] Priya Nair: One last note: instrument client-side read times — sometimes the client is the bottleneck and we end up chasing server tweaks for a client issue.
[10:45] Maya Chen: We'll add that to tracing work.
[10:49] Lena Park: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the runbook and proposed configs.

End of meeting.
